title: Apollo 11: How Humans Reached the Moon

scenes.purpose: Hook: the landing, then the question of how it was possible.

visual.title: The night the world looked up
visual.statement: On July 20, 1969, two astronauts landed on the Moon while hundreds of millions watched on live TV.

narration.text: On July 20, 1969, a fragile spacecraft called Eagle dropped toward the surface of the Moon.
Its computer was flashing alarms, and its fuel was running out.
How did people get there, only eight years after deciding to try?
It took a Cold War race,
the most powerful rocket flown up to that time,
and a landing with very little fuel to spare.

scenes.purpose: Place the space race in time.

events.label: Gagarin, the first person in space

narration.text: The race began in 1957, when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite.
In April 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
Weeks later, President Kennedy asked Congress to commit to landing on the Moon before the decade was out.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 carried three astronauts around the Moon and back.
Seven months later came Apollo 11.

scenes.purpose: Hear Kennedy's case for going.

visual.title: Because it is hard
visual.quote: We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.
visual.author: John F. Kennedy

narration.text: Kennedy sold the goal as a test of national will.
In 1962, he told a crowd at Rice University in Houston:
We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.
It was a promise, and a gamble.

scenes.purpose: Show the scale of the program.

visual.title: A nation-sized project

stats.label: people working on Apollo at its peak
total program cost at the time

visual.note: That cost is well over 200 billion dollars in today's money.

narration.text: Keeping that promise took an enormous effort.
At its peak, about four hundred thousand people worked on Apollo,
in government centers, universities and thousands of companies.
The program cost about twenty-five billion dollars at the time, well over two hundred billion today.

scenes.purpose: Define the mission plan that made Apollo possible.

visual.title: The plan that made it possible
visual.definition: A mothership waits in orbit around the Moon while a small lander goes down, then returns to meet it.
visual.example: NASA chose this plan in 1962 because it saved enormous weight.

narration.text: The first big question was how to get there at all.
NASA's answer was called lunar orbit rendezvous.
A mothership would stay in orbit around the Moon, while a small lander went down to the surface and came back up.
NASA chose this plan in 1962, because it saved enormous weight.

scenes.purpose: Show the size and power of the Saturn V.

stats.label: of propellant burned every second at launch

narration.text: To launch it all, NASA built the Saturn V, the most powerful rocket flown up to that time.
It stood one hundred eleven meters tall, about as high as a thirty-six story building.
Fully fueled, it weighed around two thousand eight hundred tonnes.
Its five first-stage engines burned about thirteen tonnes of propellant every second.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the rocket and the two spacecraft.

visual.title: A rocket and two spacecraft
visual.statement: Most of the giant stack was used up early; only one small capsule would come home.

narration.text: On top of the rocket rode two spacecraft.
The Saturn V itself would be used up in the first hours of the trip.
Columbia, the command module, was the crew's home and the only part that would return to Earth.
Eagle, the spidery lunar module, was built to land on the Moon and nowhere else.

scenes.purpose: Compare the Apollo computer with a modern phone.

visual.title: The computer that flew to the Moon

narration.text: Guiding the spacecraft was the Apollo Guidance Computer.
It had about four kilobytes of working memory, and its programs were literally woven into wire.
A modern smartphone has millions of times more memory and speed.
Yet that small computer, and the software team led by Margaret Hamilton, would prove crucial during the landing.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the crew.

visual.title: The crew
visual.statement: Three experienced test pilots, each on his second spaceflight.

narration.text: The crew were three seasoned test pilots, each on his second trip into space.
Neil Armstrong was the commander.
Buzz Aldrin would fly the lunar module down with him.
And Michael Collins would stay in orbit, flying Columbia alone.

scenes.purpose: Lay out the mission's key dates.

narration.text: Apollo 11 launched from Florida on the morning of July 16, 1969.
Three days later, it slipped into orbit around the Moon.
On July 20, Armstrong and Aldrin landed.
And on July 24, the crew splashed down in the Pacific Ocean.

scenes.purpose: Show the path from launch to lunar orbit.

narration.text: The trip followed a carefully planned path.
The Saturn V lifted the spacecraft off the pad,
and placed it in a parking orbit around Earth.
Less than three hours after launch, the third stage fired again, sending the crew toward the Moon.
Three days later, an engine burn behind the Moon slowed them into lunar orbit.

scenes.purpose: Give the distance and travel time.

narration.text: The Moon is, on average, about three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away.
Coasting most of the way, the crew took about three days to get there.

scenes.purpose: Set up the dangers of the descent.

visual.title: Twelve minutes of descent
visual.statement: The powered descent from lunar orbit to the surface took about twelve minutes, with almost no margin.

narration.text: On July 20, Eagle separated from Columbia and began its descent.
The final powered descent lasted about twelve minutes, and it did not go to plan.
The computer flashed alarms the crew had never seen in training.
The planned landing spot turned out to be strewn with boulders.
And the fuel kept running down.

scenes.purpose: Explain the 1202 alarm.

visual.title: A computer under pressure
visual.definition: The computer's warning that it was overloaded and was restarting to focus on its most urgent tasks.
visual.example: Because the software put critical tasks first, the landing could go on.

narration.text: The most famous alarm was code twelve oh two.
It meant the computer was overloaded and was restarting to focus on its most urgent jobs.
Because the software had been designed to put critical tasks first, Mission Control told the crew to keep going.

scenes.purpose: Tell the final moments before touchdown.

visual.title: Hands on the controls
visual.statement: Armstrong flew the lander by hand over a boulder field as the fuel ran down.

narration.text: Armstrong took manual control and flew Eagle past the boulders, searching for a clear spot.
In Houston, the control room went quiet as the fuel ran down.
Mission Control called out thirty seconds: soon they would have to land or abort.
Then the engine shut off, and Eagle settled into the dust.

scenes.purpose: Hear the first words from the surface.

visual.title: Tranquility Base
visual.quote: Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.
visual.author: Neil Armstrong

narration.text: Armstrong's first words from the surface were calm.
Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.
Mission Control answered that a bunch of guys had been about to turn blue, and were breathing again.

scenes.purpose: Hear the first step on the Moon.

visual.title: The first step
visual.quote: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
visual.author: Neil Armstrong

narration.text: About six and a half hours later, Armstrong climbed down the ladder.
That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
He later said he meant to say for a man, and that the word may simply have been lost.

scenes.purpose: Give the numbers of the moonwalk.

stats.label: of Moon rock and soil brought home

narration.text: An estimated six hundred million people watched on live television.
Armstrong and Aldrin spent about two and a half hours outside.
They collected about twenty-one kilograms of rock and soil to bring home.

scenes.purpose: Describe the work done on the surface.

visual.title: A busy shift on the Moon
visual.statement: The moonwalk was a tightly scheduled work shift, packed with tasks.
points: A flag and a phone call

narration.text: The moonwalk was a tightly scheduled work shift.
They planted a flag and took a phone call from President Nixon.
They set up a seismometer, and a laser reflector that scientists still use to measure the distance to the Moon.
And they gathered rocks that would help reshape ideas about how the Moon formed.
A plaque left on the lander reads: we came in peace for all mankind.

scenes.purpose: Tell Michael Collins's experience in orbit.

visual.title: Alone behind the Moon
visual.statement: While his crewmates explored, Collins circled the Moon alone, cut off from Earth on every far-side pass.

narration.text: Meanwhile, Michael Collins circled overhead in Columbia.
Each time he passed behind the Moon, he lost all radio contact with Earth.
He later wrote that he felt not fear or loneliness, but awareness, anticipation and confidence.

scenes.purpose: Show the journey home.

narration.text: Getting home was just as risky.
Eagle's upper stage lifted off, using its lower half as a launch pad and leaving it behind.
It docked with Columbia in lunar orbit, and the crew moved back aboard.
Another engine burn behind the Moon sent them home.
On July 24, they splashed down in the Pacific, southwest of Hawaii.

scenes.purpose: Show where the mission began, was run and ended.

narration.text: The mission had started at Kennedy Space Center in Florida,
and was guided throughout by Mission Control in Houston.
It ended in the Pacific, where the aircraft carrier Hornet picked up the crew.
The astronauts then spent three weeks in quarantine, in case they had brought home any Moon germs.

scenes.purpose: Summarize what Apollo achieved.

visual.title: What Apollo left behind
visual.statement: Between 1969 and 1972, six Apollo missions landed, and twelve people walked on the Moon.

narration.text: Apollo 11 was the first of six crewed landings between 1969 and 1972.
In all, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon.
The program pushed forward computing, electronics and the art of managing huge projects.
And pictures of Earth from deep space showed people how small and fragile their planet is.

scenes.purpose: Close with the legacy and the return.

visual.title: One giant leap
visual.statement: No one has walked on the Moon since December 1972, but new missions plan to return.

narration.text: No one has walked on the Moon since December 1972.
But new missions are preparing to send astronauts back, this time to stay longer.
Whatever comes next will build on that night in July 1969, when the whole world looked up.
